paragraphs: Generating a useful sequence involves two demands: it should have desirable properties, and it should obey the rules that make it valid. For discrete structures such as strings, these rules can involve syntax, meaning, and relationships between distant elements. The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing a property while keeping these complex constraints in view.

The authors formulate sequence generation as chance-constrained optimization. Here, validity is expressed through the probability that the generator produces an acceptable sequence. The objective is to keep that probability high while improving the expected property of interest. Their minimax algorithm tackles both goals together by tightening a bound on the validity probability and optimizing the property.

Experiments across three domains report better performance than existing sequence optimization methods. The contribution is a framework that treats validity as an explicit probabilistic requirement during optimization. A high validity probability does not mean every generated sequence must be valid; that distinction is part of the formulation.
icml-2020-a-chance-constrained-generativ.tldr: A generative optimization framework improves sequence properties while explicitly enforcing a high probability of validity.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization links two optimization problems: an upper-level choice depends on the solution of a lower-level problem. Many gradient-based approaches assume that each upper-level choice gives exactly one lower-level solution. This singleton assumption simplifies theory, but excludes situations in which several lower-level solutions are equally acceptable.

The paper introduces Bi-level Descent Aggregation, or BDA, to work beyond that restriction. It uses an optimistic formulation, meaning that lower-level solutions are considered with the upper-level objective in mind. The framework combines objective information from both levels and organizes the algorithm into flexible, modular components. The authors develop a convergence proof that does not require the lower-level solution to be unique.

Their proof approach also improves convergence properties for conventional first-order schemes that retain the singleton assumption. Experiments on tasks including hyperparameter optimization and meta learning support the theoretical results and report advantages for BDA. The key advance is extending convergence analysis to a broader bi-level setting, rather than treating uniqueness as indispensable.
icml-2020-a-generic-first-order-algorith.tldr: BDA combines information from both optimization levels and provides convergence guarantees without requiring a unique lower-level solution.

paragraphs: Deep residual networks can reach zero training loss despite having nonconvex optimization landscapes. This paper studies that behavior through a mean-field description, replacing a growing network with a continuous mathematical model. Its new continuum limit has a favorable property: every local minimum is also a global minimum.

The analysis connects deep residual networks to ensembles of shallow, two-layer networks. By bounding the difference between these descriptions using the adjoint sensitivity method, the authors transfer tools from shallow-network mean-field analysis to deep networks. This yields a global convergence result in the mean-field regime. The proof assumes that a global minimizer achieves zero loss, a condition the authors connect to universal approximation.

The continuous model also motivates training procedures, including one that switches the order of residual blocks and shows strong benchmark performance. The theoretical result concerns the specified continuum setting and zero-loss assumption; the empirical training results provide a separate demonstration that the mathematical viewpoint can inspire useful procedures.
icml-2020-a-mean-field-analysis-of-deep-.tldr: A new continuous model of deep ResNets supports global convergence analysis under a zero-loss assumption and inspires effective training schemes.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization represents data through factors whose entries are nonnegative. Although widely useful, existing approaches can be vulnerable when their input is deliberately perturbed. This paper develops Adversarial NMF, or ANMF, to make the factorization more robust to a broad range of noise and adversarial changes.

The model gives an adversary some control over how perturbed data are generated. It also considers potential test-time adversaries beyond predefined constraints, extending its scope beyond regular inputs or a particular prescribed noise type. The authors express this interaction as a bi-level optimization problem and solve it with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, accompanied by convergence analysis.

Under conditions described as mild, the robustness analysis establishes asymptotically unbiased prediction. Experiments report robustness across broad categories of perturbations and state-of-the-art performance on several real-world benchmark datasets. These findings support explicitly incorporating adversarial perturbations into factorization, with the theoretical claim remaining conditional and asymptotic rather than a guarantee against every possible attack.
icml-2020-adversarial-nonnegative-matrix.tldr: ANMF incorporates adversarial data perturbations into a bi-level factorization model and reports broad empirical robustness.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit repeatedly chooses among options while learning from their rewards. This paper studies rewards that combine stochastic behavior with adversarial scaling. Its motivating example is display advertising: an advertisement has a quality component that stays fixed over time, while user relevance can change non-stochastically and affects all available advertisements in the same way.

That shared variation creates a structured problem. The quality differences between options remain stable, yet the reward scale can vary in ways that standard stochastic reasoning may not handle well. The authors identify two settings in which most bandit algorithms struggle, showing that a substantial stochastic component alone does not ensure robustness.

The positive results identify two algorithms that tolerate adversarial scaling: one belongs to the action-elimination family and the other to the mirror-descent family. Their adaptability is central to the result. The study also points to broader lessons about adaptive parameter selection in stochastic bandits, without claiming that every adaptive algorithm will succeed.
icml-2020-bandits-with-adversarial-scali.tldr: The paper identifies failures under adversarial reward scaling and shows that two adaptive bandit algorithms remain robust.

paragraphs: A dialogue agent pretrained on human language can lose linguistic structure when subsequently trained only to complete a task. The paper calls this language drift: syntax and meaning deteriorate as task success becomes the dominant training signal. It proposes Seeded Iterated Learning, or SIL, as a way to counter that change.

SIL repeatedly separates task-focused improvement from imitation. A teacher is created by copying the current student and then fine-tuning that teacher for task completion. The pretrained student is periodically refined by imitating data sampled from this newly generated teacher. Repeating this process defines a training protocol that does not require external syntactic constraints or semantic knowledge.

The authors evaluate SIL in a toy Lewis Game and a natural-language translation game. In both, it helps preserve language while improving task completion relative to baselines. These results show that the two goals can improve together in the tested settings, supporting imitation-based refinement as a task-agnostic approach to fine-tuning.
icml-2020-countering-language-drift-with.tldr: Seeded Iterated Learning alternates teacher task training with student imitation to reduce language drift and improve task completion.

paragraphs: Neural networks that operate on curved spaces need operations that respect those spaces' geometry. The Fréchet mean generalizes ordinary averaging to Riemannian manifolds, but its lack of a convenient closed form and derivative has made it difficult to integrate into learning systems. This paper addresses that differentiation obstacle.

The authors show how to differentiate through the Fréchet mean on arbitrary Riemannian manifolds. They then specialize to hyperbolic space, deriving explicit gradients and a mean solver described as fast, accurate, and free of hyperparameters. Together, these components allow the geometric averaging operation to participate in a hyperbolic neural network's training pipeline.

Two case studies demonstrate the integration. Replacing projected aggregation in a Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Network produces state-of-the-art results on datasets with high hyperbolicity. A second application constructs hyperbolic batch normalization and reports an improvement analogous to its Euclidean counterpart. The work thus connects a general differentiation method to concrete neural-network operations, with the strongest reported graph results tied to the stated dataset geometry.
icml-2020-differentiating-through-the-fr.tldr: Differentiable Fréchet means enable geometry-aware averaging and batch normalization in hyperbolic neural networks.

paragraphs: Label smoothing replaces a completely concentrated training target with a mixture of that target and a uniform label distribution. It is known to help prediction and calibration empirically, but its role when training labels are already noisy is less obvious. Because smoothing is equivalent to adding symmetric label noise, it can appear to aggravate the problem.

The paper investigates this apparent tension by relating label smoothing to a broader family of loss-correction methods developed for noisy labels. That connection supplies a different way to understand what smoothing does to the learning objective. Building on it, the authors show that smoothing is competitive with loss correction under label noise.

They also study distillation from noisy data, where a student learns from a teacher model. Smoothing the teacher's labels is beneficial in this setting, contrasting with earlier findings for noise-free problems. The result makes the data's noise conditions central to interpreting smoothing's usefulness, rather than treating findings from clean-label distillation as universally applicable.
icml-2020-does-label-smoothing-mitigate-.tldr: Label smoothing connects to noise-corrected losses and can help both noisy-label learning and distillation from noisy data.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning often involves competing objectives, so one model rarely optimizes every task simultaneously. Pareto analysis studies trade-offs where improving one objective requires giving ground on another. Existing methods typically return a sparse collection of separate solutions, making it difficult to examine how nearby trade-offs connect.

This paper proposes a method for generating locally continuous Pareto sets and their corresponding objective trade-offs, or Pareto fronts. To make multi-objective theory practical at modern model sizes, the authors formulate a sample-based sparse linear system. Standard Hessian-free solvers can then be applied, providing a computational route to exploring nearby solutions.

Experiments on multi-task classification and regression show that the method identifies principal directions within local Pareto sets, efficiently discovers additional trade-offs, and scales to tasks with millions of parameters. Its value is in making local trade-off structure available for analysis and balancing. The stated scope is local continuous exploration, rather than a claim to recover every possible trade-off across the entire optimization landscape.
icml-2020-efficient-continuous-pareto-ex.tldr: A scalable method explores continuous local Pareto trade-offs between tasks instead of returning only isolated solutions.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching makes singular value decomposition practical for very large matrices by working with smaller representations. The resulting singular values and vectors are approximations, however, and users need to know how far they may be from the exact quantities. Computing an approximation is therefore only part of the practical problem.

The paper develops a data-driven bootstrap method to estimate these errors numerically. Its target is the error associated with the particular matrix and sketch being used. This addresses a weakness of relying on analytical worst-case bounds, which may fail to reflect the structure of an individual problem and can encourage unnecessary computation.

The method operates entirely on sketched objects, so error estimation requires no additional passes over the full matrix. That design keeps the extra computation inexpensive and preserves a central benefit of sketching. The contribution is a practical way to assess approximation quality alongside the approximate decomposition, helping users judge the accuracy of the result they have actually computed.
icml-2020-error-estimation-for-sketched-.tldr: A bootstrap method estimates sketched SVD errors cheaply using only the sketch, without rereading the full matrix.

paragraphs: Dense neural networks can demand substantial memory and energy, motivating methods that retain fewer connections while remaining trainable. Many approaches select those connections using labels from a particular task. Neural Tangent Transfer instead seeks sparse networks without using labels to decide which network structure to retain.

The method matches aspects of a sparse network's training behavior to those of a dense network. It characterizes that behavior through the neural tangent kernel, which describes training dynamics in the space of functions represented by the network. The selection target is therefore how the sparse model learns, rather than a label-dependent pruning score.

Evaluations on several standard classification tasks report higher classification performance and faster convergence for the resulting sparse networks. The label-free claim concerns finding the sparse networks; the paper still evaluates them on classification tasks. Its contribution is to use similarity in learning dynamics as a criterion for sparsification, connecting structural compression to the ability to train effectively.
icml-2020-finding-trainable-sparse-netwo.tldr: Neural Tangent Transfer finds sparse networks without labels by matching dense-network training dynamics.

paragraphs: Visual planning learns goal-directed behavior from previously collected observations, such as images of robot interactions. This paper plans directly with images by organizing them into a graph: images become nodes, learned connections describe possible transitions, and conventional graph search produces a plan. This gives the planned route an explicit visual form.

The method extends semi-parametric topological memory in two ways. First, an energy-based connectivity function is trained using contrastive predictive coding, providing stable training. Second, a conditional variational autoencoder generates images from a description of the domain. These generated images supply graph nodes, allowing the system to construct plans in new domains without prior interaction there.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art visual planning methods in plan interpretability and in success when a trajectory-following controller executes the plan. They also find that the method can account for nontrivial object properties, including geometry. The results connect image generation to planning through a searchable graph, while keeping the intermediate plan visually inspectable.
icml-2020-hallucinative-topological-memo.tldr: Generated domain-conditioned images form a searchable planning graph that improves visual interpretability and controller success in new domains.

paragraphs: PageRank measures node importance in a graph, and very large graphs motivate distributing its computation. In that setting, efficiency depends both on how many communication rounds are needed and on how much information nodes exchange during each round. This paper improves the second quantity while preserving the asymptotic order of the first.

The comparison uses a generalized congested clique computation model. For n nodes and a constant d of at least one, the existing Radar-Push method approximates PageRank with relative error of order 1/(log n)^d. It takes O(log log n + log d) rounds, but its bandwidth can reach O((log n)^(2d+3)) bits between a pair of nodes per round.

The new algorithm uses asymptotically the same number of rounds while requiring only O(d(log n)^3) bits of bandwidth. This sharply reduces the stated bandwidth dependence on graph size and the parameter d. The contribution is a theoretical communication improvement within the specified distributed model, where round count alone would conceal a substantial cost.
icml-2020-improved-communication-cost-in.tldr: A distributed PageRank algorithm reduces asymptotic bandwidth requirements while retaining the previous communication-round complexity.

paragraphs: Algebraic multigrid is a fast approach to solving large sparse linear systems, a recurring task in science and engineering. Its efficiency depends heavily on the prolongation operator, a sparse matrix governing the solver's multiscale hierarchy. Choosing that operator is problem-dependent, and established methods do not provide one universally correct choice.

The paper learns this component with a graph neural network. Its framework targets systems whose matrices are sparse, symmetric, and positive definite or positive semidefinite. A single network learns a mapping from an entire class of such matrices to prolongation operators, using an efficient unsupervised loss. Learning is thus directed at a critical part of an existing numerical solver.

Across a broad class of experimental problems, the learned operators produce better convergence rates than classical algebraic multigrid. These results suggest that neural networks can help design effective sparse-system solvers by adapting their internal operators to the matrix class. The evidence concerns improved solver convergence in the tested problems, within the stated matrix setting.
icml-2020-learning-algebraic-multigrid-u.tldr: A graph neural network learns multigrid prolongation operators that improve convergence on a broad class of sparse linear systems.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Kernel-based tests answer this using a measure of similarity between observations. The paper learns that similarity with a deep neural network, training it specifically to improve the test's ability to detect distributional differences.

The learned kernels can adapt to how distribution shape and smoothness vary across the data space. This is more flexible than adjusting only the lengthscale of a spatially homogeneous kernel, and is particularly relevant to complex, high-dimensional data. The framework also includes popular classifier-based two-sample tests as a special case, while offering improvements beyond that case.

The authors provide a consistency proof for their adaptation method, covering deep-feature kernels as well as radial basis kernels and multiple kernel learning. Experiments on benchmark and real-world data report superior testing performance. The work combines a more expressive learned comparison rule with theoretical support for the adaptation process used to construct the test.
icml-2020-learning-deep-kernels-for-non-.tldr: Deep learned kernels adapt two-sample tests to complex distribution differences, with consistency guarantees and improved empirical test performance.

paragraphs: Models such as Transformers need an explicit way to represent token position because they do not process inputs sequentially like recurrent networks. Common choices create a trade-off: fixed sinusoidal encodings have no learnable parameters, while position embeddings restrict the maximum sequence length. The paper seeks a position representation that is both adaptable and able to extend across input lengths.

Its solution models the evolution of positional encodings as a continuous dynamical system. Drawing on Neural ODEs, the authors learn how the encoding changes along the position index. This provides parameters that can adapt to different datasets and architectures while supporting extrapolation as the input length varies.

Experiments on neural machine translation and language understanding tasks report consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution places a learned continuous process inside the position layer, connecting flexibility and variable-length encoding in one design. The reported task improvements support that design without establishing that extrapolation will succeed equally well for every possible sequence length.
icml-2020-learning-to-encode-position-fo.tldr: A learned continuous dynamical system encodes token positions and improves results on translation and language understanding tasks.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries from partially observed data. This paper targets a median matrix using absolute deviation loss. Although the median has appealing properties, the loss is nonsmooth, making large-scale optimization challenging. Dividing the work into independent parallel computations is straightforward, but the resulting estimators can be statistically inefficient.

The authors introduce a refinement step based on pseudo data to improve those initial estimators. The refinement turns an inefficient parallel estimate into a matrix completion procedure with an optimal or near-optimal statistical rate. Its role is to recover estimation quality while starting from the computationally convenient parallel approach.

The refined result approximates a regularized least median estimator, rather than being an ordinary regularized empirical-risk estimator itself. That distinction requires a nonstandard analysis of its asymptotic behavior. Empirical results also support the method's effectiveness. The paper therefore addresses both sides of the large-data problem: obtaining an initial estimate through parallel computation and refining it enough to achieve strong statistical accuracy.
icml-2020-median-matrix-completion-from-.tldr: A pseudo-data refinement makes parallel median matrix completion statistically optimal or near-optimal.

paragraphs: Min-max optimization couples variables that seek opposite outcomes from an objective. This paper considers constrained problems where the optimizer can query objective values but cannot access gradients. That black-box setting makes ordinary gradient-based descent and ascent unavailable directly, while still allowing information to be gathered through evaluations.

The proposed ZO-Min-Max framework estimates gradients from a small number of function queries. It combines this zeroth-order estimator with alternating projected stochastic descent and ascent, using one-step updates. Projection handles the constraints. Under conditions described as mild, the authors establish a sublinear convergence rate and report favorable scaling with problem size.

The paper also connects this framework to black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning. Empirical evaluations on these applications demonstrate effectiveness at dimensions that make recent black-box solvers impractical. The results give both conditional convergence support and application evidence for solving competing-objective problems when function values, rather than derivatives, are the accessible source of information.
icml-2020-min-max-optimization-without-g.tldr: ZO-Min-Max solves constrained black-box min-max problems using function-query gradient estimates and alternating descent-ascent updates.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent distributes training across participants that exchange information. Reducing the precision of those messages can lower communication costs, but the resulting quantization must still support effective optimization. Moniqua is a technique for adding quantized communication to a variety of decentralized training algorithms.

The authors prove that Moniqua uses a bounded number of communicated bits per iteration while preserving the original algorithm's asymptotic convergence rate with full-precision communication. It requires no additional memory and can operate with one-bit quantization. These properties address communication, storage, and optimization behavior together rather than judging compression by message size alone.

Experiments show faster convergence in wall-clock time than other quantized decentralized algorithms. In training ResNet20 and ResNet110 on CIFAR10, one bit per parameter is sufficient without compromising validation accuracy. This accuracy finding is tied to those experiments, while the convergence result concerns asymptotic rates. Together, they support very low-precision communication as a practical option for the evaluated decentralized training settings.
icml-2020-moniqua-modulo-quantized-commu.tldr: Moniqua enables low-bit decentralized SGD communication while preserving asymptotic convergence rates and reporting faster wall-clock convergence.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation addresses the mismatch between the data used to learn a model and the data it later encounters. In open-set adaptation, the target data also contain classes absent from the source. This makes the problem broader than aligning two distributions that contain exactly the same object categories.

The paper introduces Progressive Graph Learning, an end-to-end framework combining a graph neural network with adversarial learning. Episodic training of the graph component is used to suppress conditional shift, while adversarial learning reduces the gap between source and target distributions. The framework therefore combines mechanisms aimed at different aspects of the mismatch.

The authors establish a tighter upper bound on target error than existing open-set adaptation approaches. They also report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on three standard open-set benchmarks. The bound and experiments provide distinct support: one improves the theoretical characterization of target error, while the other demonstrates better observed performance in settings that include previously unseen target classes.
icml-2020-progressive-graph-learning-for.tldr: Progressive Graph Learning combines episodic graph training and adversarial adaptation to handle target domains containing additional classes.

paragraphs: In partial-label learning, each training example comes with several candidate labels, exactly one of which is correct. The learner must improve its predictions while resolving that ambiguity. Existing methods often rely on specialized constrained optimization procedures, whose computational cost can make large datasets difficult to handle.

This paper develops a classification-risk estimator and analyzes its classifier consistency and estimation error. It then proposes a progressive identification algorithm that approximately minimizes the estimator. Updating the predictive model and identifying the true labels occur within the same learning process, linking label disambiguation directly to model improvement.

The resulting algorithm is independent of a particular model or loss and works with stochastic optimization. These properties make the framework flexible about the learning machinery used underneath it, addressing the dependence on specialized solvers. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines statistical analysis of the learning objective with a practical procedure for training under candidate-label ambiguity.
icml-2020-progressive-identification-of-.tldr: A flexible risk estimator and progressive label-identification algorithm support scalable learning from ambiguous candidate labels.

paragraphs: Smooth games arise when interacting objectives must be optimized together, as in adversarial machine learning. This paper studies stochastic Hamiltonian methods for such games and introduces an unbiased estimator for stochastic Hamiltonian gradient descent, or SHGD. It uses optimization tools to establish convergence guarantees for specified classes of games.

The analysis shows linear convergence to a neighborhood of a stationary point. To obtain convergence to the exact solution, the authors analyze decreasing step sizes and introduce a stochastic variance-reduced Hamiltonian method. This distinguishes rapidly approaching a region around a solution from eliminating the remaining error.

The guarantees concern the final iterate, hold globally, and give finite-time bounds for stochastic unconstrained bilinear games and games satisfying a sufficiently bilinear condition. That broader class includes some nonconvex, nonconcave problems. Experiments on these game classes show the theory to be tight, and additional experiments examine simple adversarial learning formulations. The results expand the provable scope of stochastic game optimization without claiming coverage of all smooth games.
icml-2020-stochastic-hamiltonian-gradien.tldr: Stochastic Hamiltonian methods gain last-iterate convergence guarantees for bilinear and sufficiently bilinear games.

paragraphs: Fairness-constrained classification seeks a predictor that satisfies a chosen definition of nondiscrimination. A common strategy replaces the original fairness constraint with a relaxed version that is easier to optimize. This paper examines whether satisfying such a replacement actually delivers the fairness it is intended to represent.

The authors show that many existing relaxations can be misleading: a model may meet the relaxed constraint while remaining substantially unfair under the relevant notion. The problem is a gap between the optimization condition being enforced and the desired property of the resulting classifier. Successful optimization of the replacement condition alone does not resolve that gap.

The proposed framework uses a strongly convex formulation and supplies theoretical guarantees on the fairness of its solution. Experiments on real data give promising results. The contribution is to connect the tractable optimization problem more securely to the fairness requirement, with the guarantee understood relative to the chosen fairness notion rather than as a universal definition of fair behavior.
icml-2020-too-relaxed-to-be-fair-623e81c.tldr: Common relaxed fairness constraints can permit unfair classifiers; a strongly convex alternative provides theoretical fairness guarantees.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate underlying factors of variation in observations. This paper studies learning from related image pairs that share at least one factor. The pairs are not independent observations: their relationship provides weak supervision about what remains stable and what changes.

The theoretical result shows that knowing how many factors changed is sufficient for learning disentangled representations, even without knowing which factors changed. The practical algorithms go further in their annotation requirements: they use image pairs without labels identifying groups, individual factors, or the number of changes. The sufficient information used in the theoretical statement should therefore be distinguished from what the algorithms require as input.

A large empirical study finds that paired observations support reliable disentanglement on several benchmark datasets. The learned representations are also useful across tasks involving covariate shifts, fairness, and abstract reasoning. These findings support paired environmental observations as a way to learn representations with several downstream benefits, while retaining the stated assumption that each pair shares an underlying factor.
icml-2020-weakly-supervised-disentanglem.tldr: Related image pairs provide weak supervision for learning disentangled representations useful across several downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making requires an agent to connect current observations with information retained from earlier steps. Working Memory Graphs explore whether Transformer-style attention can improve that process. The proposed agent applies multi-head self-attention to a changing collection of vectors representing both observations and recurrent state.

The evaluation covers three environments with factored observations, where inputs are presented as separable components. Pathfinding emphasizes reasoning over past observations, BabyAI gridworld levels introduce variable goals, and Sokoban emphasizes future planning. This collection tests the architecture across different demands on memory and decision-making rather than a single kind of task.

Across all evaluated tasks, the combination of the attention-based architecture and factored observation spaces yields significant gains in learning efficiency over baseline architectures. The finding ties the benefit to both the model and the input structure. It demonstrates that Transformer-based agents can substantially improve sample efficiency in reinforcement-learning environments whose observations can be factored, rather than establishing the same gain for every observation format.
icml-2020-working-memory-graphs-c713bdc1.tldr: Working Memory Graphs use attention over observations and recurrent state to improve learning efficiency in environments with factored inputs.
